label: Transversals and Epsilon Nets
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 231 to 264, asks how a small finite witness can certify a property of an entire range space. We open with the twin goals: piercing every heavy range with an epsilon-net, and stabbing a whole family of convex sets with a small transversal of points.

label: Set Systems and Ranges
notes: A range space pairs a ground set with a family of admissible subsets, for instance points pierced by halfplanes or disks. Counting how many distinct ranges a finite point set can carve out is the combinatorial quantity that controls every sampling theorem appearing later in this chapter.

label: Shattering and VC Dimension
notes: A set is shattered when every one of its subsets is cut out by some range. The VC dimension is the size of the largest shattered set, a single integer that measures the combinatorial richness of the range space and bounds its complexity throughout the sampling arguments.

label: The Shatter Function and Sauer-Shelah
notes: Sauer and Shelah prove that bounded VC dimension forces the shatter function to grow only polynomially, never exponentially. This polynomial ceiling is the structural miracle that makes random sampling work, turning a potentially exponential family of ranges into a tame object we can union-bound over.

label: Epsilon-Nets
notes: An epsilon-net is a subset of the ground set that meets every range heavier than an epsilon fraction of the measure. It is a guarantee of coverage: no large region escapes the net, even though the net itself may be tiny compared with the entire ground set.

label: The Epsilon-Net Theorem
notes: Haussler and Welzl show that for a range space of VC dimension d, a random sample of size proportional to d over epsilon times the logarithm of one over epsilon is an epsilon-net with high probability. The size depends on dimension and epsilon, never on the ground set.

label: Why Random Sampling Works
notes: The proof uses a double-sample and a symmetrization argument. We compare the true sample with a ghost sample, bound the bad event by the polynomial shatter function from Sauer-Shelah, and the union bound closes because polynomial growth is crushed by the exponential decay of the miss probability.

label: Epsilon-Approximations
notes: An epsilon-approximation is stronger than a net: it preserves the relative density of every range up to an additive epsilon, not merely nonemptiness. Such samples let us estimate how heavy any range is, which underpins discrepancy bounds and the efficient approximate range counting met at the chapter's end.

label: Transversals and Piercing
notes: A transversal, or piercing set, is a set of points meeting every member of a family of convex sets. Epsilon-nets supply transversals for the heavy part of a family, and Helly-type hypotheses control when a small piercing number is guaranteed to exist for the whole collection.

label: Weak Epsilon-Nets
notes: A weak epsilon-net may use points outside the ground set to pierce every heavy convex range. Dropping the membership restriction buys dramatically smaller nets for convex ranges, with bounds independent of the number of points, a cornerstone of selection lemmas and centerpoint-style results.

label: Hadwiger-Debrunner (p,q)
notes: The Hadwiger-Debrunner problem asks: if among every p convex sets some q have a common point, is the whole family pierced by few points? Alon and Kleinman answered yes, and their proof leans on fractional Helly together with the epsilon-net machinery developed across this chapter.

label: Application: Range Searching
notes: In range searching we preprocess points to answer how many lie in a query halfplane or box. Epsilon-approximations shrink the data while preserving counts, and bounded VC dimension certifies that the approximate structure stays small and provably accurate, the practical dividend of the whole chapter.

label: Recap and Compass
notes: The chapter's logic is a chain: VC dimension bounds the shatter function, Sauer-Shelah makes it polynomial, sampling then yields epsilon-nets and approximations, and those feed transversals, weak nets, and Hadwiger-Debrunner piercing. Carry that dependency map into the exercises and test it on disks in the plane.
